authoredFrom: SOL-5 — `is` is not always `extends`. Authored 2026-09-30 from the analyzer's measured output. This fixture exists because `extends` had 537 corpus rows and ZERO fixture rows: all-kinds-sol's heritage edges all name an interface, so the kind was exercised only by a corpus measurement, which is not a gate.
note: BOTH kinds appear in one file, and that is the whole design: a rule that always emitted `extends` would fail the `implements` row, and a rule that always emitted `implements` would fail the `extends` row, so neither can pass by accident. Solidity's heritage list has NO `interface` keyword — `contract C is A, B` is the only form — so the tree does not say which kind each ancestor is and the distinction comes from the ancestor's own declaration, resolved within this file. `FeedBase is IFeed` is `implements` because `IFeed` is an `interface_declaration` here; `Feed is FeedBase` is `extends` because `FeedBase` is a `contract_declaration`. `override(FeedBase)` on `Feed.latest` names its base EXPLICITLY, which is the case Solidity gives the analyzer and PowerShell never did — the target inside that base is still located by matching, so the tier is `inferred`. SOL-19 added a third shape to this file: a base NOT declared here, whose kind is therefore undecided. The three together are the whole ruling — settled by the tree (1.0/structural), settled as a non-interface by an in-file declaration (1.0/structural), and undecided because the declaration is elsewhere (0.9/inferred + flag).

forbidSymbols.name: is
forbidSymbols.comment: SOL-5's trap in name form: `is` is the heritage KEYWORD and reaches the graph as a bare `identifier`. A callee pass that treated any identifier under an expression as a call would publish `calls -> is`. It is refused by the derived reserved-token rule, which is why that rule exists as a derived set rather than a remembered list.

forbidSymbols.name: override
forbidSymbols.comment: The `override` keyword, same shape as `is`. Solidity keywords are reserved tokens and no project can declare them.

forbidSymbols.name: super
forbidSymbols.comment: `super.latest()` resolves the PROPERTY as the call target, and `super` is a global object rather than a project member, so SOL-7 silences it as a member read.

expectRelationships.comment: SOL-5, the `implements` half. `FeedBase is IFeed` and `IFeed` is an `interface_declaration` in THIS file, so the kind is settled by the ancestor's own declaration rather than by anything in the heritage list.

SOL-5, the `extends` half, and the row this fixture was written for: the kind had 537 corpus rows and no fixture row at all. `FeedBase` is an abstract CONTRACT, so this is implementation inheritance rather than interface satisfaction.

SOL-11. `override(FeedBase)` NAMES the base, which the grammar settles — Solidity has the keyword where PowerShell had nothing. The TARGET inside that base is located by matching the member name, so the tier is `inferred` and not `structural`. Measured on the corpus: 8 emitted against 386 unresolved, because a base declared in another file yields NO edge at all rather than a fabricated one, and the unresolved count is reported rather than hidden.

An override resolved from the CONTRACT HEADER rather than an explicit list — `FeedBase is IFeed` with a bare `override`. The metadata distinguishes the two shapes, so a reader can tell which bases were named and which were inferred from the heritage list.

A BASE CONSTRUCTOR INVOCATION. `constructor() FeedBase() {}` is a `modifier_invocation`, which grammar.js gives no field at all, so the name is the first `identifier` child. 204 of them exist in the corpus and a callee pass over `call_expression` alone would publish none of them — the base-constructor half of `extends` would simply be missing.

`super.latest()` — a call THROUGH a global object. SOL-7 silences a global's member READ (`msg.sender` names no project member) but keeps a CALL through one, because `latest` IS a project function and `super.f()` is how Solidity reaches a base implementation. The edge's source and target happen to share a name because the enclosing function and the overridden one are both `latest`; that is what the source says.
`abstract contract FeedBase` — the `abstract` keyword is read off the node's FIRST child token rather than by matching source text, so `meta.isAbstract` is a structural fact and not a substring hit.

SOL-19. `IOther` is not declared here, so the tree does not say whether it is an interface. The edge is still emitted — omitting a TRUE inheritance edge to avoid annotating an uncertain KIND would trade a labelled fact for a silence — but the claim is marked: 0.9, tier `inferred`, `kindUnresolved`, and the kind that was ASSUMED. It was published at 1.0/`structural` before, which is the overstatement this row exists to prevent: a consumer weighting by tier read a guess as a fact, and one filtering `extends` to find contracts inherited a mis-typed base.

forbidRelationships.comment: THE ROW THAT MAKES SOL-5 A DECISION. `IFeed` is an interface, so this is `implements`. A rule that relabelled every interface base as `extends` would lose no edge and change no total — only the KIND — which is why this forbid row exists alongside the `implements` row and the count below.

The mirror image: `FeedBase` is a contract, so implementation inheritance is `extends`. Pins that the rule is not 'implements for the first base' — a positional guess would get both of these backwards relative to the file's own declarations.
SOL-7: `super` is a global object, not a project member. The call's TARGET is the property `latest`, which is what the expect row above pins.
SOL-7 again, the read side. `super` cannot be declared by a project, so a `uses` edge naming it is a fabrication by construction.

A SELF-TARGET: `Feed.latest` does not override a member of itself. `override(FeedBase)` names a base, and the resolution skips `base === owner` so a diamond-inheritance header that lists the deriving contract cannot produce an edge a function overrides in its own owner. This file's `Feed` does not list itself, so the row is absent rather than wrong — and it is forbidden so the skip stays load-bearing.

The same row from the other side: the undecided-kind population must never be reported at full confidence. `confidenceMin: 0.99` is the assertion; a single FORBID row for the CONFIDENCE is what stops the tier from being fixed while the number is not.

The IN-FILE case must keep full confidence. `IFeed` is an `interface_declaration` in this file, so its kind is settled by the tree and downgrading it would be the opposite error — reporting a fact as a guess.

expectRelationshipCount.comment: One interface base in the file. A rule that emitted `implements` for every heritage edge would report 2 and fail here.

Two contract bases: `Feed is FeedBase`, whose kind the tree SETTLES, and `CrossFile is IOther`, whose kind it cannot settle because IOther is declared in another file. Both are `extends`; they differ in CONFIDENCE and TIER, which is the point of SOL-19 — a count that cannot tell them apart cannot gate either.

FeedBase overrides both interface functions (resolved from the heritage list), and Feed overrides FeedBase's `latest` (resolved from the explicit `override(FeedBase)`). A rule that ignored the explicit list and matched any same-named member in any ancestor would add `overrides feedKind -> FeedBase`... which does not exist because `Feed` does not declare `feedKind`, so this count is also what pins that a member is only overridden if it is actually DECLARED in the base. CrossFile's bare `override` resolves against its SINGLE header base IOther (SOL-11's one-base rule), which is the fourth.
